# 04.0 Building a Complete HTML Page

Now that you know the basic skeleton of an HTML document, let's fill it in with content! In this lesson, you'll learn how to add headings, paragraphs, links, and images to your web pages. You'll also master the art of nesting and indentation — skills that keep your code clean and easy to read.

## Recap: The HTML Skeleton

Remember the four essential parts of every HTML page:

- `<!DOCTYPE html>` — tells the browser this is an HTML5 document
- `<html>` — the root element that wraps everything
- `<head>` — contains metadata like the page title
- `<body>` — holds all visible content

In the previous lesson, you built a page with just a title. Now we'll add real content inside the `<body>`.

## Headings and Paragraphs

Headings create hierarchy on your page, just like chapters in a book. HTML offers six levels of headings:

- `<h1>` — main title (use only once per page)
- `<h2>` to `<h6>` — subheadings, in decreasing importance

Paragraphs are created with the `<p>` tag. They automatically add space above and below the text.

```html
<h1>My Travel Blog</h1>
<p>This is my first blog post about my trip to Paris.</p>
```

> **Tip:** Always use headings to structure your content logically. Screen readers and search engines rely on them to understand your page.

## Links with the Anchor Tag

The `<a>` tag (anchor) creates clickable links. To specify where the link goes, you use the `href` attribute. To make the link open in a new browser tab, add `target="_blank"`.

```html
<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank">Read More</a>
```

Notice how the attribute (`target="_blank"`) is placed inside the opening tag, separated by a space. This is the standard way to add attributes to any HTML element.

## Images with the Img Tag

The `<img>` tag embeds images. It's a **void element** — it doesn't have a closing tag. It uses two essential attributes:

- `src` — the image URL (where the image is located)
- `alt` — alternative text describing the image (important for accessibility and when the image doesn't load)

```html
<img src="https://picsum.photos/400/300" alt="A random travel photo">
```

> **Important:** Always include `alt` text. It helps visually impaired users and improves SEO.

## Putting It All Together: Nesting and Indentation

Now let's combine everything in a complete page. Notice how each element is **nested** inside the `<body>` and indented with two spaces to show its parent-child relationship.

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My Travel Blog</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>My Travel Blog</h1>
    <p>This is my first blog post about my trip to Paris.</p>
    <img src="https://picsum.photos/400/300" alt="A random travel photo">
    <a href="https://example.com" target="_blank">Read More</a>
  </body>
</html>
```

Key rules:
- **Nesting:** Elements inside other elements are indented to show the hierarchy.
- **Closing order:** The most recently opened tag must close first. For example, if you had a link inside a paragraph, you'd close `</a>` before `</p>`.
- **Indentation:** Use 2 spaces per level. It makes your code much easier to read and debug.

## Summary

In this lesson, you learned:

- How to add **headings** (`<h1>`) and **paragraphs** (`<p>`) to structure text
- How to create **links** with the `<a>` tag and the `href` and `target` attributes
- How to embed **images** with the `<img>` tag and the `src` and `alt` attributes
- Why **nesting** and **indentation** matter for clean, maintainable code

You're now ready to build a simple but complete web page. In the next lesson, you'll explore more elements and start styling your pages!
